newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gold price will wander in next few years, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Gold price will wander in next few years, experts say.

text.p: Many bullion industry experts gathered here for a two-day international gold conference have been expressing distinctly downbeat views on the metal's price trend over the next couple of years.

This was despite two days of presentations at the conference, organised by ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, showing gold mines in Australia, Latin America, Canada and Asia with new reserves and production set to reap the fruits of hundreds of millions of dollars in investment.
"We are neutral on gold." said the host company's director of research in Australia David Walker.

He wasn't alone. Several delegates representing leading mining companies, banks and stockbrokers saw little in the way of "blue skies" to directly encourage the miners' efforts at least through to the end of next year.

The gold bullion price took another jolt this week as stock values soared in the U.S. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 135.26 points to close on Tuesday at 6,587.16, its second biggest one-day rise ever, after encouraging U.S. inflation data.
Gold meanwhile slipped to around U.S. $341 per ounce continuing a slide which began on Friday when U.S. inflation figures came out below expectations.

In fact bullion has been losing value for months ever since the European central banks began looking at their gold reserves as a means of raising cash to meet the entry criteria for European Monetary Union.

One Europe-based banker taking a longer term backward glance noted, "Anybody who has investment in gold in the past 10 years has lost money. That's why the level of private client interest in gold is decreasing every day."

The prospect of at least threats of sales from the huge vaults of the central banks would keep the market on the defensive through the current quarter of 1997 and probably in the second half of the year as well, according to ABN-AMRO's Walker.
"By 1998 there may be a marginal recovery in prices," Walker said, citing lessening central bank interest as a factor behind a slightly firmer market.
Even so, the pace will not be electrifying. "We see the price wandering back up to around $390.00 over the next couple of years," Walker said.

But Walker cautioned that it remained to be seen how the gold price would react to the prolonged period of low inflation the major economies were experiencing with only minor signs of inflation showing on the U.S, horizon.
Traditionally in times of high inflation and economic growth gold prices have risen strongly as investors view it as a hedge.
"There is no reason to invest in gold at the moment when paper assets are so strong, so why should the price go up?" one delegate said.
Not that the miners were greatly dismayed. Most of them demonstrated a cost of production of under $300 an ounce, providing a healthy operating margin.
"The margin is what you run your business on," said Chris Lalor, executive director of Sons of Gwalia mine, one of Australia's major produders represented at the conference.

Lalor's company has protected and boosted its profit margin by selling gold not even mined yet at current prices plus interest. "Our policy of forward selling has been proved absolutely right," he said.
As at November 30 last year, the company had two million ounces of gold sold forward representing 58 percent of existing and probable reserves.
"Forward selling undoubtedly helps the producers flatten out variations in the spot gold price," said Walker.

ABN-AMRO research indicated Sons of Gwalia had total procution costs of A$462 last year but through its hedging policy received an average gold price of A$665 against an average spot gold price of A$514. Estimates show this year's margin's to be as healthy.
